name: Radiating Star in de Sitter Space
description: A spherical source of null radiation in a spacetime with a positive cosmological constant.
convention: We work in units with $G = c = 1$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A radiating spherical body sits in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. In outgoing null coordinates its spacetime has the line element $ds^2=-\left(1-2m(u)/r-\Lambda r^2/3\right)du^2-2\,du\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2$, where $u$ is retarded time, $r$ is the areal radius, and $m(u)$ is the mass in units of length [campos2025cosmological, mallett1985radiating]. Ronald L. Mallett presented an exact solution for a radiating body in a de Sitter background in 1985 [campos2025cosmological, mallett1985radiating].¶The radiation travels along outgoing null surfaces $u=\mathrm{constant}$. The outgoing energy density is nonnegative when $m'(u)\leq 0$, and the mass is nonincreasing [senovilla2023ultramassive, campos2025cosmological]. The mass falls as outgoing radiation carries energy away, with $8\pi T_{uu}=-2m'(u)/r^2$ in units $G=c=1$ [senovilla2023ultramassive, campos2025cosmological].¶The same family admits an ingoing null description with advanced time $v$ and mass $m(v)$ [senovilla2023ultramassive]. When $m'(v)\geq 0$, the incoming null radiation satisfies the dominant energy condition and the mass is nondecreasing [senovilla2023ultramassive]. A decreasing mass in advanced time describes an inward flux of negative energy, a model used for evaporation near a black hole [mbonye1999horizons].¶Mallett studied an evaporating black hole during inflation in 1986, following its apparent and event horizons [mbonye1999horizons, mallett1986erratum, mallett1986evolution]. Manasse R. Mbonye extended the analysis to higher dimensions, following the apparent and event horizons of the black hole and the cosmological region for negative ingoing energy [mbonye1999horizons]. In the ingoing description, the apparent horizons lie at the positive roots of $1-2m(v)/r-\Lambda r^2/3=0$ [mbonye1999horizons]. For $0<9\Lambda m^2<1$ there are two such radii, associated with the black hole and the cosmological region [senovilla2023ultramassive]. The event horizons depend on the global evolution and need not coincide with those instantaneous radii [senovilla2023ultramassive, mbonye1999horizons].¶José M. M. Senovilla studied incoming radiation that builds up the mass of a black hole in a de Sitter background [senovilla2023ultramassive]. In his model, the two marginally trapped tubes meet when $9\Lambda m^2=1$. If the incoming mass rises beyond this threshold, the resulting spacetime has a future singularity reached by every observer in the model [senovilla2023ultramassive].¶Thiago de L. Campos, C. Molina, and J. A. S. Lima studied the mass loss as seen by cosmological observers [campos2025cosmological]. They followed a family of observers constructed from curves that comove in de Sitter space. In their evaporation model, some of these observers see a nonzero mass even as their cosmological time tends to infinity [campos2025cosmological].

related.text: A constant mass in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. With $m$ constant, the radiation vanishes.
The background with $m=0$, a universe with a positive cosmological constant.
A spherical radiating body with charge and no cosmological constant. Its mass and charge can vary with retarded time [bonnor1970].

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass as a function of null time, measured as a length

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded null coordinate $u$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(u)$ is a function of $u$ alone. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass as a function of null time, measured as a length

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced null coordinate $v$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(v)$ is a function of $v$ alone. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
